requirements: Reproduce the core contributions of 'Quantization-Aware Distillation for NVFP4 Inference Accuracy Recovery', demonstrating that QAD recovers near-BF16 accuracy for NVFP4-quantized LLMs and VLMs across SFT-heavy and RL-heavy post-trained models, with robustness to data quality and coverage.

sub_tasks.requirements: Hardware, software, and NVFP4 format infrastructure required to run QAD experiments are available and correctly configured.
GPU hardware and CUDA/driver stack supporting NVFP4 arithmetic (Blackwell-class or equivalent emulation) are available.

Code has been implemented to detect and report the presence of GPUs capable of running NVFP4 (Blackwell architecture) or a fallback emulation mode; the setup script verifies hardware capability before launching training.
Code has been implemented to configure the CUDA toolkit, cuDNN, and NCCL versions compatible with NVFP4 kernels (e.g., CUDA 12.x with Transformer Engine or equivalent) and log the versions used.
Training framework infrastructure (Megatron-LM, NeMo, and HuggingFace Transformers variants) is set up to support QAD experiments as referenced in the abstract.
Code has been implemented to install and initialize Megatron-LM with NVFP4 QAD support, including the fake-quantization or true-quantization forward-pass modules for GEMM layers.
Code has been implemented to install and initialize the NeMo training framework with the QAD training recipe modules used in the paper.
Code has been implemented to install a HuggingFace Transformers variant capable of loading NVFP4-quantized checkpoints for inference/evaluation.
NVFP4 format is correctly implemented with the block structure and two-level scaling specified in Section 2.1.
Code has been implemented for the NVFP4 format using a block size of 16 elements (as opposed to 32 for MXFP4), with each block having its own scale factor.
Code has been implemented so that per-block scale factors are stored in E4M3 (FP8) format, providing non-power-of-two scaling factors.
Code has been implemented for a per-tensor FP32 second-level scale factor that extends the dynamic range of NVFP4 tensors beyond the E4M3 block scales.

The NVFP4 quantize/dequantize routines behave correctly on unit tests: quantizing then dequantizing a tensor produces values within the expected FP4 representable set, and the max absolute error scales appropriately with the block E4M3 scale.
Quantization is applied only to the forward pass of GEMM layers as specified for QAT/QAD (Figure 2, Appendix D), with gradients kept in high precision.

Code has been implemented so that Fprop GEMMs use NVFP4 inputs (activation and weight) while Wgrad and Dgrad GEMMs operate in high precision (BF16/FP32), matching the QAT/QAD compute graph in Figure 2.
Master weights are maintained in FP32 during QAD/QAT training, with NVFP4 weight quantization applied only in the forward pass; unit tests confirm optimizer updates occur on FP32 master weights.
Distributed training and mixed-precision infrastructure to run models up to 49B parameters (or Mixture-of-Experts up to 30B-A3B) is configured.
Code has been implemented to enable tensor/pipeline/expert parallelism sufficient for training Llama Nemotron Super V1 (49B) and Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B (MoE) with NVFP4 forward-pass quantization.

Code has been implemented to load teacher (BF16) and student (NVFP4-quantized) models simultaneously on device with sufficient memory management (activation checkpointing, teacher inference-only forward pass without gradients).

All teacher models (Llama Nemotron Super V1, Nemotron Nano 9B V2, Nemotron Nano 12B V2 VL, Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B, AceReason Nemotron 1.1 7B) and training/evaluation datasets are available and correctly loaded for QAD experiments.
BF16 teacher model checkpoints for all five studied models are acquired and loadable.

Code has been implemented to download and load the AceReason Nemotron 1.1 7B BF16 checkpoint (Qwen2.5-based, specialized for math and code via RL).
Loaded teacher models expose a forward-pass API returning full BF16 vocabulary-sized logits suitable for KL divergence distillation.

Data preparation pipeline correctly tokenizes and packs training data for each model with appropriate tokenizers and sequence lengths matching each model's original post-training configuration.

Post-training quantization to NVFP4 is implemented with the correct selective-quantization policy for each model architecture, reproducing PTQ baseline numbers.
NVFP4 PTQ quantization machinery (calibration and selective layer quantization) is implemented.

Code has been implemented that performs post-training quantization of an LLM's linear/GEMM layers to NVFP4 format using max-based calibration on a small representative dataset without any weight fine-tuning.

Code has been implemented that supports a per-layer selective quantization policy, allowing specified layers (e.g., attention layers, first/last layers, Mamba layers) to remain in BF16 while others are quantized to NVFP4.
Code has been implemented that supports FP8 KV-cache quantization as an optional configuration alongside NVFP4 weight/activation quantization.
The selective quantization policies specified per model architecture are correctly configured.
For Llama Nemotron Super V1 and AceReason Nemotron 1.1 7B, all GEMM layers are quantized to NVFP4 with no BF16-preserved layers.

For Nemotron Nano 9B V2 (hybrid Mamba-Transformer with 4 Transformer layers and 52 Mamba layers), all attention layers in Transformer blocks and the first two and last two layers are kept in BF16 while the remaining GEMMs are quantized to NVFP4.
For Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B, all 6 self-attention layers and their preceding Mamba-2 layers are kept in BF16, the remaining network is quantized to NVFP4, and the KV-Cache is quantized to FP8.
For Nemotron Nano 12B V2 VL, the NVFP4 PTQ configuration mirrors the same selective quantization policy used for the LLM component of the VLM.
NVFP4 numerical format details (block size 16, E4M3 per-block scale, FP32 per-tensor scale) are correctly implemented in the PTQ path.
The NVFP4 quantizer uses a block size of 16 elements (rather than 32 as in MXFP4) for both weights and activations.
The NVFP4 quantizer applies two-level scaling: per-block E4M3 (FP8) scale factors and a per-tensor FP32 scale factor.
Measured NVFP4 PTQ baseline accuracies match the reported numbers for the primary models.
NVFP4 PTQ on Llama Nemotron Super V1 achieves MATH500=91.4, AIME25=32.3, GPQA-D=62.1, IFEval-Instruction=86.9 (Table 2).
NVFP4 PTQ on Nemotron Nano 9B V2 achieves MATH500=97.2, AIME25=69.8, GPQA-D=59.0, IFEval-Instruction=89.8 (Table 2).
NVFP4 PTQ on Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B achieves AA-LCR=31.3, AIME25=85.0, GPQA-D=71.6, LiveCodeBench-v5=68.9, SciCode=30.5 (Table 3a).
NVFP4 PTQ on AceReason Nemotron 1.1 7B achieves AIME24=69.4, AIME25=58.7, LiveCodeBench-v6=52.0 (Table 3b).
The PTQ baseline accuracy drops on small models are non-negligible compared to BF16 (e.g., Llama Nemotron Super V1 AIME25 drops from 46.0 to 32.3), demonstrating the sensitivity that motivates QAD.
Quantization-aware training with next-token cross-entropy loss on NVFP4-quantized forward pass is implemented as the baseline comparison method.
The QAT training loop with next-token cross-entropy loss and quantized forward pass is implemented.

Code has been implemented that defines a QAT training routine which quantizes the student model's forward pass to NVFP4 while keeping weights in a high-precision master copy and gradients in high precision.

Code has been implemented that computes a next-token cross-entropy loss between the NVFP4-quantized student's output logits and the ground-truth token labels from the training data (no teacher model used in the loss).
Code has been implemented that applies a straight-through estimator (or equivalent) so gradients flow through the NVFP4 quantization operations in the forward pass during QAT backpropagation.
The QAT compute graph quantizes only weights and activations in the forward (Fprop) pass; the Wgrad and Dgrad GEMMs remain in high precision, matching Figure 2's QAT diagram.
QAT is configured with the same selective-quantization policies, data pipelines, and hyperparameters as QAD so the two are directly comparable.
Code has been implemented so that QAT runs use the identical NVFP4 selective-quantization configuration (which layers are kept in BF16 vs quantized) as the corresponding QAD run for each model.
Code has been implemented so QAT uses the same training data mixture, batch size, sequence length, and token count as the paired QAD run for each model (SFT-heavy and RL-heavy).

Code has been implemented that supports running QAT with the same conservative learning rates listed for QAD (1e-6 for Llama Nemotron Super V1 and Nemotron Nano 9B V2; 1e-5 for AceReason Nemotron and Nemotron 3 Nano).
Checkpoint selection for QAT follows the same validation-loss-based procedure used for QAD.
Code has been implemented that evaluates the top-10 QAT checkpoints with the lowest validation cross-entropy loss and selects the one with the best average benchmark accuracy.
QAT behaves as described relative to QAD: it can match validation cross-entropy but shifts the output distribution away from the BF16 teacher.

Code has been implemented that, given a trained QAT checkpoint and a held-out evaluation set, computes both the token-level cross-entropy loss vs labels and the KL divergence of the QAT student's output distribution vs the BF16 teacher's output distribution.

On Llama Nemotron Super V1 trained on ~0.3B tokens sampled from its SFT dataset and evaluated on 5,000 held-out samples (~8M tokens), QAT's cross-entropy vs labels matches the BF16 baseline value of 0.408 (paper reports 0.408 for QAT).

On the same Llama Nemotron Super V1 setup, QAT's KL divergence vs the BF16 teacher is significantly non-zero and matches the paper's reported value of 0.311, in contrast to QAD's near-zero KL of 0.004.
QAT is applied and evaluated across all the model families where it serves as a comparison baseline for QAD.
Code has been implemented that runs the NVFP4 QAT baseline end-to-end on the SFT-heavy models (Llama Nemotron Super V1 and Nemotron Nano 9B V2) using their SFT data mixtures.

Code has been implemented that runs the NVFP4 QAT baseline on the RL-heavy models (Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B and AceReason Nemotron 1.1 7B) using cold-start SFT data (and, for Nemotron 3 Nano, a mixture with RL-generated data).
Code has been implemented that runs the NVFP4 QAT baseline on Nemotron Nano 12B V2 VL and evaluates it on the VLM benchmark suite reported in Appendix A.
Quantization-aware distillation with KL divergence loss between BF16 teacher and NVFP4 student is correctly implemented per Section 3.1.
Overall QAD training pipeline architecture with teacher-student setup is structurally implemented.

Code has been implemented that instantiates a full-precision BF16 teacher model (loaded from the original post-trained checkpoint) and a separate quantized NVFP4 student model, with the teacher and student sharing the same architecture and initial weights.
Code has been implemented that keeps the teacher model in BF16 with parameters frozen (no gradient updates) throughout QAD training.

Code has been implemented that applies NVFP4 fake-quantization to the student's forward pass (weights and activations of quantized GEMM layers) while keeping backward-pass gradients in high precision (i.e., only Fprop is quantized; Wgrad and Dgrad remain in high precision), matching the compute graph in Figure 2.

Code has been implemented that on each training step performs a forward pass through both the teacher (BF16) and the student (NVFP4-quantized) on the identical input batch to produce two logit tensors of matching shape (batch, seq_len, vocab_size).
KL divergence loss between teacher and student output distributions is correctly implemented per Section 3.1.
Code has been implemented that computes softmax probability distributions p_teacher(y|x) and p_student(y|x) over the vocabulary V from the raw logits of teacher and student respectively.

Code has been implemented that computes the KL divergence loss KL(p_teacher || p_student) (forward KL with teacher as reference distribution) averaged over tokens as the sole training objective for QAD.
The softmax temperature T is set to 1 for both teacher and student when computing distributions for the KL loss, as specified in Section 3.4.
Code has been implemented that ensures gradients flow only through the student branch of the KL loss (teacher logits are detached / not part of the autograd graph).
On a small synthetic batch, when teacher and student logits are set equal, the computed KL divergence loss evaluates to (approximately) zero, confirming correct loss computation.
The QAD training objective uses ONLY the KL divergence loss with no additional cross-entropy label term (contrasting with QAT which uses next-token cross-entropy).
Loss masking and token alignment are handled correctly for the distillation objective.

Code has been implemented that applies a shift+mask to align next-token positions and masks out padding/prompt tokens from the KL loss computation, matching the 'Shift + Mask' block shown in Figure 1.
Code has been implemented that averages the KL divergence over non-masked tokens (rather than summing across all positions including padding).
Training loop for QAD is correctly implemented with optimizer updates only on student parameters.

Code has been implemented that constructs the optimizer with only the student model's trainable parameters (teacher parameters excluded), and calls loss.backward() followed by optimizer.step() on each step.

Code has been implemented that tracks a held-out validation KL loss during training and saves the top-10 checkpoints with the lowest validation loss (used later for evaluation selection per Section 3.4).
Code has been implemented that supports batch sizes and sequence lengths configured to be similar to those used in the original post-training of the corresponding model.
The QAD implementation is validated end-to-end by reproducing the reference Table 1 diagnostic on Llama Nemotron Super V1.

The QAD-trained Llama Nemotron Super V1 student achieves KL divergence vs the BF16 teacher of approximately 0.004 (near-zero) on the held-out 5,000-sample evaluation set, matching Table 1.
The QAD-trained Llama Nemotron Super V1 student achieves cross-entropy vs labels of approximately 0.416 on the held-out 5,000-sample evaluation set, matching Table 1.

The Table 1 comparison demonstrating that QAD achieves near-zero KL divergence from the BF16 teacher while QAT diverges significantly, despite both matching cross-entropy loss, is reproduced on Llama Nemotron Super V1.
The evaluation setup for the alignment comparison is implemented.
Code has been implemented to train Llama Nemotron Super V1 with QAD and QAT using approximately 0.3B tokens sampled from the model's SFT dataset for this alignment experiment.
Code has been implemented to construct a held-out evaluation set of 5,000 samples (~8M tokens) from the SFT dataset, disjoint from the training data.

Code has been implemented to compute per-token KL divergence between the student model's output distribution and the BF16 teacher's output distribution across the held-out evaluation set, aggregated to a single scalar.
Code has been implemented to compute next-token cross-entropy loss versus ground-truth labels on the held-out evaluation set for BF16, QAT, and QAD checkpoints.
Code has been implemented to evaluate KL divergence and cross-entropy for three configurations - BF16 baseline, NVFP4 QAT, and NVFP4 QAD - using identical evaluation data and tokenization.
The measured KL divergence values from Table 1 are reproduced.
The KL divergence of the BF16 baseline versus itself is 0 (Table 1).
The KL divergence of NVFP4 QAT versus BF16 teacher on the Llama Nemotron Super V1 held-out set matches the paper value of 0.311 (Table 1).
The KL divergence of NVFP4 QAD versus BF16 teacher on the Llama Nemotron Super V1 held-out set matches the paper value of 0.004 (Table 1), demonstrating near-zero divergence.
The measured cross-entropy values from Table 1 are reproduced.
The cross-entropy of the BF16 baseline versus labels on the Llama Nemotron Super V1 held-out set matches the paper value of 0.408 (Table 1).
The cross-entropy of NVFP4 QAT versus labels matches the paper value of 0.408 (Table 1), demonstrating QAT matches BF16 validation loss.
The cross-entropy of NVFP4 QAD versus labels matches the paper value of 0.416 (Table 1).

The qualitative alignment claim - QAD KL divergence is substantially lower than QAT KL divergence while QAT and QAD have comparable cross-entropy - is verified in the reproduced results, demonstrating that QAT changes the output distribution while QAD preserves it.
